claim: BNP treatment increases heart function after myocardial infarction
source: Brain natriuretic peptide (BNP) treatment increases heart function and decreases heart dilation after myocardial infarction (MI).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known finding that provides context for the study

claim: BNP treatment decreases heart dilation after myocardial infarction
source: Brain natriuretic peptide (BNP) treatment increases heart function and decreases heart dilation after myocardial infarction (MI).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known finding

claim: BNP treatment increased vascularisation in all areas of infarcted hearts
source: BNP treatment increased vascularisation and the number of endothelial cells in all areas of infarcted hearts.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figures 2 and 3

claim: BNP treatment increased the number of endothelial cells in all areas of infarcted hearts
source: BNP treatment increased vascularisation and the number of endothelial cells in all areas of infarcted hearts.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by flow cytometry and western blot data in Figure 2

claim: BNP directly stimulated the proliferation of resident endothelial cells
source: Endothelial cell lineage tracing showed that BNP directly stimulated the proliferation of resident endothelial cells via NPR-A binding and p38 MAP kinase activation.
evidence: This is supported by lineage tracing experiments in Figure 5 and in vitro experiments in Figure 4

claim: BNP stimulates endothelial cell proliferation via NPR-A binding
source: Endothelial cell lineage tracing showed that BNP directly stimulated the proliferation of resident endothelial cells via NPR-A binding and p38 MAP kinase activation.
evidence: This is supported by experiments using NPR-A knockout mice shown in Figure 4C

claim: BNP stimulates endothelial cell proliferation via p38 MAP kinase activation
source: Endothelial cell lineage tracing showed that BNP directly stimulated the proliferation of resident endothelial cells via NPR-A binding and p38 MAP kinase activation.
evidence: This is supported by western blot analysis of p38 phosphorylation in Figure 6D

claim: BNP stimulated the proliferation of WT1+ epicardium-derived cells only in the hypoxic area of infarcted hearts
source: BNP also stimulated the proliferation of WT1+ epicardium-derived cells but only in the hypoxic area of infarcted hearts.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining and cell counting data in Figure 7

claim: WT1+ epicardium-derived cells have a natural capacity to differentiate into endothelial cells in infarcted hearts
source: Our results demonstrated that these immature cells have a natural capacity to differentiate into endothelial cells in infarcted hearts.
evidence: This is supported by lineage tracing experiments using WT1:ROSA mice shown in Figure 8

claim: BNP treatment increased WT1+ cell proliferation but not their differentiation capacity
source: BNP treatment increased their proliferation but not their differentiation capacity.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 8 showing increased numbers but similar differentiation percentages

claim: Increased vascularisation supports heart recovery after ischemia
source: Increased vascularisation supports heart recovery after ischemia.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction

claim: Formation of new vessels in the hypoxic area restores blood flow
source: The formation of new vessels in the hypoxic area restores blood flow, provides oxygen and nutriments to the surviving cells, and promotes the migration and engraftment of new cells.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction

claim: Angiogenic inhibition contributes to the development of heart failure in cardiac injury animal models
source: While angiogenic inhibition contributes to the development of heart failure in cardiac injury animal models, early heart reperfusion or increased angiogenesis improves cardiac function and delays the onset of heart failure in patients suffering from cardiac ischemia (Shiojima et al., 2005; Friehs et al., 2006; Tirziu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Early heart reperfusion improves cardiac function in patients suffering from cardiac ischemia
source: While angiogenic inhibition contributes to the development of heart failure in cardiac injury animal models, early heart reperfusion or increased angiogenesis improves cardiac function and delays the onset of heart failure in patients suffering from cardiac ischemia (Shiojima et al., 2005; Friehs et al., 2006; Tirziu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Increased angiogenesis delays the onset of heart failure in patients suffering from cardiac ischemia
source: While angiogenic inhibition contributes to the development of heart failure in cardiac injury animal models, early heart reperfusion or increased angiogenesis improves cardiac function and delays the onset of heart failure in patients suffering from cardiac ischemia (Shiojima et al., 2005; Friehs et al., 2006; Tirziu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Angiogenesis is the main mechanism of neovascularisation in adult infarcted hearts
source: Angiogenesis is the main mechanism of neovascularisation in adult infarcted hearts (Manavski et al., 2018; Li et al., 2019; Ray et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies

claim: After myocardial infarction, angiogenesis in the infarct border zone occurs by clonal expansion of pre-existing resident endothelial cells with no EndMT mechanism
source: The current consensus is that after myocardial infarction (MI), angiogenesis in the infarct border zone of the heart occurs by clonal expansion of pre-existing resident endothelial cells with no EndMT mechanism (Manavski et al., 2018; Li et al., 2019; He et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies

claim: The molecular pathway involved in myocardial neovascularisation after ischemia remains unknown
source: However, the molecular pathway involved in myocardial neovascularisation after ischemia remains unknown.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the introduction

claim: The developmental VEGFA-MEF2 pathway is impaired in adult ischaemic hearts
source: Indeed, Payne et al., 2019 recently demonstrated that the developmental VEGFA-MEF2 pathway, which was thought to be involved, is in fact impaired in adult ischaemic hearts.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Payne et al., 2019

claim: WT1+ epicardial cells migrate from the epicardium to the myocardium during heart development
source: Epicardial cells, and more precisely, cells expressing the Wilms' tumour 1 transcription factor (WT1) migrate from the epicardium to the myocardium during heart development and then differentiate into coronary endothelial cells, pericytes, smooth muscle cells, and even cardiomyocytes after epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (Zhou et al., 2008; Cano et al., 2016; Smits et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies

claim: WT1+ cells differentiate into coronary endothelial cells during heart development
source: Epicardial cells, and more precisely, cells expressing the Wilms' tumour 1 transcription factor (WT1) migrate from the epicardium to the myocardium during heart development and then differentiate into coronary endothelial cells, pericytes, smooth muscle cells, and even cardiomyocytes after epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (Zhou et al., 2008; Cano et al., 2016; Smits et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Numerous WT1+ cells are found in foetal and neonatal hearts
source: Consequently, numerous WT1+ cells are found in foetal and neonatal hearts, whereas only a few cells express WT1 in adult hearts (Duim et al., 2016; Duim et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Only a few cells express WT1 in adult hearts
source: Consequently, numerous WT1+ cells are found in foetal and neonatal hearts, whereas only a few cells express WT1 in adult hearts (Duim et al., 2016; Duim et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Numerous proliferating WT1+ cells can be localised in the epicardium near the infarct and border zone in hypoxic adult hearts
source: In hypoxic adult hearts, numerous proliferating WT1+ cells can be localised in the epicardium near the infarct and border zone, suggesting that hypoxia stimulates either the proliferation of the remaining WT1+ cells or the re-expression of WT1 in cardiac cells (Duim et al., 2015; Balbi et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies

claim: WT1+ epicardium-derived cells remain in a thickened layer on the heart surface without migrating into the myocardium in adult hearts after MI
source: WT1+ epicardium-derived cells (EPDCs) remain in a thickened layer on the heart surface without migrating into the myocardium or differentiating into other cell types such as cardiomyocytes or endothelial cells (Zhou et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhou et al., 2011

claim: Injections of thymosin beta four fail to induce WT1+ cell differentiation into endothelial cells in adult hearts after MI
source: Different treatments (e.g. injections of thymosin beta four or human amniotic fluid stem cell secretome) fail to induce WT1+ cell differentiation into endothelial cells in adult hearts after MI (Balbi et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies

claim: BNP supplementation after ischaemic damage promotes the recovery of cardiac function in adult rodent ischaemic hearts
source: In the last few years, we and others reported that BNP supplementation after ischaemic damage promotes the recovery of cardiac function and prevents cardiac remodelling in adult rodent ischaemic hearts (Bielmann et al., 2015; Moilanen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies

claim: BNP supplementation prevents cardiac remodelling in adult rodent ischaemic hearts
source: In the last few years, we and others reported that BNP supplementation after ischaemic damage promotes the recovery of cardiac function and prevents cardiac remodelling in adult rodent ischaemic hearts (Bielmann et al., 2015; Moilanen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies

claim: LCZ696 treatment leads to reduced rate of mortality in patients suffering from heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
source: Furthermore, in clinic, a treatment (LCZ696 or Entresto, Novartis) based on inhibition of neprilysin, an enzyme involved in the degradation of the natriuretic peptides, leads to reduced rate of mortality in patients suffering from heart failure with reduced and preserved cardiac contractility or ejection fraction (McMurray et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to McMurray et al., 2014

claim: BNP stimulates in vitro the proliferation of cardiac non-myocyte cells expressing Sca-1
source: Curiously, we observed that BNP stimulates in vitro and in vivo (i.e. in adult infarcted hearts) the proliferation of cardiac non-myocyte cells (NMCs) expressing the stem cell antigen-1 (Sca-1) (Rignault-Clerc et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rignault-Clerc et al., 2017

claim: BNP stimulates in vivo the proliferation of cardiac non-myocyte cells expressing Sca-1 in adult infarcted hearts
source: Curiously, we observed that BNP stimulates in vitro and in vivo (i.e. in adult infarcted hearts) the proliferation of cardiac non-myocyte cells (NMCs) expressing the stem cell antigen-1 (Sca-1) (Rignault-Clerc et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rignault-Clerc et al., 2017

claim: Sca-1+ cells in adult hearts are pure endothelial cells
source: As Sca-1+ cells in adult hearts were reported to be pure endothelial cells (Zhang et al., 2018), we questioned whether BNP modulates endothelial cell fate.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2018

claim: High BNP levels in plasma are associated with increased collateral development in patients with coronary artery disease
source: Thus, since high BNP levels in plasma are associated with increased collateral development in patients with coronary artery disease (Xi et al., 2011), this work aimed to determine whether part of the cardioprotective effect of BNP treatment after experimental MI involves increased neovascularisation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Xi et al., 2011

claim: BNP treatment had no significant effect on systolic blood pressure at the doses used
source: In previous work, we first controlled that with the doses of BNP used, we had no effect on systolic blood pressure (measured every day) (Bielmann et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work

claim: BNP treatment had no significant effect on heart rate in infarcted mice
source: Secondly, we evaluated cardiac parameters and heart structure by echocardiography in BNP and saline-treated 'unmanipulated' and infarcted mice. No difference was detected in heart rate, cardiac output, left ventricular diastolic volume (LV Vol;d) as well as for the index of systemic vascular resistance between both groups, demonstrating that BNP treatment (at the dose used in this study) had no significant effect on volumia and no peripheral vascular effect (Bielmann et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work

claim: BNP treatment had no significant effect on cardiac output in infarcted mice
source: Secondly, we evaluated cardiac parameters and heart structure by echocardiography in BNP and saline-treated 'unmanipulated' and infarcted mice. No difference was detected in heart rate, cardiac output, left ventricular diastolic volume (LV Vol;d) as well as for the index of systemic vascular resistance between both groups, demonstrating that BNP treatment (at the dose used in this study) had no significant effect on volumia and no peripheral vascular effect (Bielmann et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work

claim: BNP treatment had no peripheral vascular effect at the dose used
source: Secondly, we evaluated cardiac parameters and heart structure by echocardiography in BNP and saline-treated 'unmanipulated' and infarcted mice. No difference was detected in heart rate, cardiac output, left ventricular diastolic volume (LV Vol;d) as well as for the index of systemic vascular resistance between both groups, demonstrating that BNP treatment (at the dose used in this study) had no significant effect on volumia and no peripheral vascular effect (Bielmann et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work

claim: Contractility was twofold increased 4 weeks after MI in BNP-treated groups
source: Third, contractility (EF@LV Vol;d) was twofold increased 4 weeks after MI in BNP-treated groups and BNP injections reduced clearly heart remodelling (which is the percentage of changes of the left ventricle volume) 1 (−45%, p=0.06) and 4 weeks (−79%, p=0.04) after MI (Bielmann et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work

claim: BNP injections reduced heart remodelling 1 week after MI by 45%
source: Third, contractility (EF@LV Vol;d) was twofold increased 4 weeks after MI in BNP-treated groups and BNP injections reduced clearly heart remodelling (which is the percentage of changes of the left ventricle volume) 1 (−45%, p=0.06) and 4 weeks (−79%, p=0.04) after MI (Bielmann et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work

claim: BNP injections reduced heart remodelling 4 weeks after MI by 79%
source: Third, contractility (EF@LV Vol;d) was twofold increased 4 weeks after MI in BNP-treated groups and BNP injections reduced clearly heart remodelling (which is the percentage of changes of the left ventricle volume) 1 (−45%, p=0.06) and 4 weeks (−79%, p=0.04) after MI (Bielmann et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work

claim: BNP treatment reduced mRNA levels coding for vimentin in the RZ of infarcted hearts 1 week after MI by 59%
source: Accordingly, BNP treatment of infarcted hearts reduced also mRNA levels coding for vimentin in the RZ of infarcted hearts 1 (−59%, p=0.004) and 4 (-36%, p=0.025) weeks after MI, which suggests an effect on fibrosis development as already demonstrated by other (Moilanen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work

claim: BNP treatment reduced mRNA levels coding for vimentin in the RZ of infarcted hearts 4 weeks after MI by 36%
source: Accordingly, BNP treatment of infarcted hearts reduced also mRNA levels coding for vimentin in the RZ of infarcted hearts 1 (−59%, p=0.004) and 4 (-36%, p=0.025) weeks after MI, which suggests an effect on fibrosis development as already demonstrated by other (Moilanen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work

claim: Most BNP effects after MI depend on cardiac rather than on vascular effects
source: Altogether, these results clearly demonstrated that most BNP effects after MI depend on cardiac rather than on vascular effects.
evidence: This is inferred from the data presented in Figure 1 and previous work

claim: Intraperitoneal BNP injections increased cardiac cGMP levels 3.13-fold 30 minutes after injection
source: BNP acts directly on the heart. Indeed, very rapidly after intraperitoneal (ip) BNP injections (i.e. 30 min), increased cGMP levels were detected by ELISA in cardiac tissue (x 3.13, p=0.006) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA measurements shown in Figure 1B

claim: In the plasma of unmanipulated mice, cGMP concentration increased 3.8-fold after one BNP injection
source: In the plasma of unmanipulated mice, cGMP concentration increased 3.8-fold (103 vs 25 pmoles/ml) after one BNP injection (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA measurements shown in Figure 1C

claim: In infarcted mice, 1 day after BNP injection, the plasmatic cGMP concentration remained high (207 vs 51 pmoles/ml)
source: In infarcted mice, 1 day after BNP injection, the plasmatic cGMP concentration remained high (207 vs 51 pmoles/ml, p=0.05) (Figure 1C), but returned to the level detected in the plasma of saline-injected mice 2 days after BNP injection (data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA measurements shown in Figure 1C

claim: The pPLB/PLB ratio increased 2.1-fold in unmanipulated hearts 1 to 3 hr after BNP injection
source: The pPLB/PLB ratio increased 2.1-fold in 'unmanipulated' hearts 1 to 3 hr after BNP injection (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by western blot analysis shown in Figure 1D

claim: In infarcted hearts of BNP-treated mice, the pPLB/PLB ratio increased 2.1-fold in the ZI+BZ 3 days after MI
source: In infarcted hearts of BNP-treated mice, the pPLB/PLB ratio increased 3 days after MI, 2.1- and 1.5-fold in the infarct and border zone (ZI+BZ) and in the remote zone (RZ), respectively.
evidence: This is supported by western blot analysis shown in Figure 1D

claim: In infarcted hearts of BNP-treated mice, the pPLB/PLB ratio increased 1.5-fold in the RZ 3 days after MI
source: In infarcted hearts of BNP-treated mice, the pPLB/PLB ratio increased 3 days after MI, 2.1- and 1.5-fold in the infarct and border zone (ZI+BZ) and in the remote zone (RZ), respectively.
evidence: This is supported by western blot analysis shown in Figure 1D

claim: 10 days after MI, the pPLB/PLB ratio increased 4.0-fold in the ZI+BZ of BNP-treated hearts
source: 10 days after MI, the pPLB/PLB ratio increased 4.0-fold in the ZI+BZ and was unchanged in the RZ.
evidence: This is supported by western blot analysis shown in Figure 1D

claim: The pPLB/PLB ratio increased 197-fold in NMCs isolated from the ZI+BZ of infarcted hearts in BNP-treated mice 10 days after MI
source: Furthermore, the pPLB/PLB ratio increased 197- and 179-fold in NMCs isolated from the ZI+BZ and RZ of infarcted hearts in BNP-treated mice 10 days after MI (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by western blot analysis shown in Figure 1E

claim: The pPLB/PLB ratio increased 179-fold in NMCs isolated from the RZ of infarcted hearts in BNP-treated mice 10 days after MI
source: Furthermore, the pPLB/PLB ratio increased 197- and 179-fold in NMCs isolated from the ZI+BZ and RZ of infarcted hearts in BNP-treated mice 10 days after MI (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by western blot analysis shown in Figure 1E

claim: Intraperitoneal injections of BNP can target cardiac NMCs
source: According to these results, intraperitoneal injections of BNP can target cardiac NMCs.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing increased pPLB/PLB ratio in isolated NMCs

claim: Endothelial cells in infarcted hearts express NPR-A and NPR-B
source: Endothelial cells in infarcted hearts express NPR-A and NPR-B (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining and flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: mRNA levels coding for CD31 increased 1.3-fold in cells isolated from RZ of BNP-treated infarcted hearts 3 days after MI
source: Increased mRNA levels coding for CD31 (x 1.3, p=0.025) and Ve-cadherin (x 1.3, p=0.07) were detected in the cells isolated from RZ of BNP-treated infarcted hearts 3 days after MI (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2A

claim: mRNA levels coding for Ve-cadherin increased 1.3-fold in cells isolated from RZ of BNP-treated infarcted hearts 3 days after MI
source: Increased mRNA levels coding for CD31 (x 1.3, p=0.025) and Ve-cadherin (x 1.3, p=0.07) were detected in the cells isolated from RZ of BNP-treated infarcted hearts 3 days after MI (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2A

claim: 10 days after MI, mRNA levels coding for vWF increased 1.5-fold in the ZI+BZ after BNP treatment
source: 10 days after MI, mRNA levels coding for vWF (x 1.5, p=0.023), VeCad (x 1.4, p=0.0007) and eNOS (x 1.4, p=0.049) were increased in the ZI+BZ after BNP treatment (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2A

claim: 10 days after MI, mRNA levels coding for VeCad increased 1.4-fold in the ZI+BZ after BNP treatment
source: 10 days after MI, mRNA levels coding for vWF (x 1.5, p=0.023), VeCad (x 1.4, p=0.0007) and eNOS (x 1.4, p=0.049) were increased in the ZI+BZ after BNP treatment (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2A

claim: 10 days after MI, mRNA levels coding for eNOS increased 1.4-fold in the ZI+BZ after BNP treatment
source: 10 days after MI, mRNA levels coding for vWF (x 1.5, p=0.023), VeCad (x 1.4, p=0.0007) and eNOS (x 1.4, p=0.049) were increased in the ZI+BZ after BNP treatment (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2A

claim: The number of CD31+ cells increased 100% in the RZ 3 days after MI following BNP treatment
source: The number of CD31+ cells increased in the RZ (+ 100%) 3 days after MI following BNP treatment (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2C

claim: A higher number of CD31+ cells was found 10 days after MI in the ZI+BZ (+29%) of BNP-treated hearts
source: A higher number of CD31+ cells was found 10 days after MI in the ZI+BZ (+29%, p=0.04) and RZ (+28%, p=0.01) of BNP-treated hearts (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2C

claim: A higher number of CD31+ cells was found 10 days after MI in the RZ (+28%) of BNP-treated hearts
source: A higher number of CD31+ cells was found 10 days after MI in the ZI+BZ (+29%, p=0.04) and RZ (+28%, p=0.01) of BNP-treated hearts (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2C

claim: CD31 protein levels were 26% higher in the ZI+BZ of BNP-treated hearts compared to saline-injected hearts 10 days after MI
source: CD31 protein levels were higher in the ZI+BZ (+26%, p=0.06) and RZ (+69%, p=0.0003) of BNP-treated hearts compared to saline-injected hearts 10 days after MI (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2D

claim: CD31 protein levels were 69% higher in the RZ of BNP-treated hearts compared to saline-injected hearts 10 days after MI
source: CD31 protein levels were higher in the ZI+BZ (+26%, p=0.06) and RZ (+69%, p=0.0003) of BNP-treated hearts compared to saline-injected hearts 10 days after MI (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2D

claim: Cardiac vascularisation increased 2.2-fold 3 days after MI in the RZ of BNP-treated hearts
source: Cardiac vascularisation increased 2.2-fold 3 days after MI in the RZ (p=0.002) of BNP-treated hearts, while it remained unchanged in the ZI+BZ.
evidence: This is supported by CD31 staining intensity measurements shown in Figure 3B

claim: BNP treatment increased cardiac vascularisation 108% in the ZI+BZ 10 days after MI
source: BNP treatment increased cardiac vascularisation 10 after MI in the ZI+BZ (+ 108%, p=0.02) and RZ (+76%, p=0.002) (Figure 3A–B).

claim: BNP treatment increased cardiac vascularisation 76% in the RZ 10 days after MI
source: BNP treatment increased cardiac vascularisation 10 after MI in the ZI+BZ (+ 108%, p=0.02) and RZ (+76%, p=0.002) (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: This is supported by CD31 staining intensity measurements shown in Figure 3A-B

claim: 4 weeks after MI, vascularisation remained 1.7-fold increased in BNP-treated hearts
source: 4 weeks after MI, vascularisation remained 1.7-fold increased in BNP-treated hearts.
evidence: This is supported by CD31 staining intensity measurements shown in Figure 3B

claim: A 2.0-fold increase in CD31+ cells was counted 3 days after MI in the ZI+BZ of BNP-treated hearts compared to saline-injected hearts
source: We counted CD31+ cells on heart slices after immunostaining (Figure 3C), observing a 2.0 and 1.8-fold increase 3 days after MI in the ZI+BZ (p=0.003) and RZ (p=0.024) of BNP-treated hearts compared to saline-injected hearts, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by cell counting data shown in Figure 3C

claim: A 1.8-fold increase in CD31+ cells was counted 3 days after MI in the RZ of BNP-treated hearts compared to saline-injected hearts
source: We counted CD31+ cells on heart slices after immunostaining (Figure 3C), observing a 2.0 and 1.8-fold increase 3 days after MI in the ZI+BZ (p=0.003) and RZ (p=0.024) of BNP-treated hearts compared to saline-injected hearts, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by cell counting data shown in Figure 3C

claim: A 1.4-fold increase in CD31+ cells was counted 10 days after MI in the ZI+BZ of BNP-treated mice
source: A 1.4- and 2-fold increase in CD31+ cells was counted 10 days after MI in the ZI+BZ (p=0.02) and RZ (p=0.05) of BNP-treated mice, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by cell counting data shown in Figure 3C

claim: A 2-fold increase in CD31+ cells was counted 10 days after MI in the RZ of BNP-treated mice
source: A 1.4- and 2-fold increase in CD31+ cells was counted 10 days after MI in the ZI+BZ (p=0.02) and RZ (p=0.05) of BNP-treated mice, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by cell counting data shown in Figure 3C

claim: A 1.8-fold increase in CD31+ cells was counted 28 days after MI in the ZI+BZ of BNP-treated mice
source: This was also the case 28 days after MI (ZI+BZ: x 1.8, and RZ: x 2) (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by cell counting data shown in Figure 3C

claim: A 2-fold increase in CD31+ cells was counted 28 days after MI in the RZ of BNP-treated mice
source: This was also the case 28 days after MI (ZI+BZ: x 1.8, and RZ: x 2) (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by cell counting data shown in Figure 3C

claim: mRNA levels coding for von Willbrand factor were upregulated in neonatal BNP-treated cells compared to untreated cells
source: mRNA levels coding for von Willbrand factor, Ve-cadherin, and eNOS were upregulated in neonatal BNP-treated cells compared to untreated cells (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4A

claim: mRNA levels coding for Ve-cadherin were upregulated in neonatal BNP-treated cells compared to untreated cells
source: mRNA levels coding for von Willbrand factor, Ve-cadherin, and eNOS were upregulated in neonatal BNP-treated cells compared to untreated cells (Figure 4A).

claim: mRNA levels coding for eNOS were upregulated in neonatal BNP-treated cells compared to untreated cells
source: mRNA levels coding for von Willbrand factor, Ve-cadherin, and eNOS were upregulated in neonatal BNP-treated cells compared to untreated cells (Figure 4A).

claim: BNP treatment increased the number of CD31+ cells by 41% in adult NMCs in vitro
source: BNP treatment increased the number of CD31+ cells in vitro (+87% and +41% in neonatal and adult NMCs, respectively) (Figure 4C).

claim: The increase in CD31+ cells after BNP treatment completely disappeared in the NMCs isolated from NPR-A knockout mouse hearts

claim: BNP binds to NPR-A to increase the number of endothelial cells
source: The increase in CD31+ cells after BNP treatment completely disappeared in the NMCs isolated from the NPR-A knockout mouse model (Npr1 KO) but not from NPR-B KO hearts (Npr2 KO hearts) (+56%, p=0.04), suggesting that BNP binds to NPR-A to increase the number of endothelial cells (Figure 4C).

claim: The percentage of CD45+ cells among the CD31+ cell subset was less than 10% in all zones of the infarcted hearts 3 and 10 days after MI

claim: The numbers and percentages of CD45+ and CD31+ cells were similar in BNP- and saline-treated hearts 3 and 10 days after MI

claim: The increased number of CD31+ cells in BNP-treated hearts was not due to infiltrating cells
source: The increased number of CD31+ cells in BNP-treated hearts was thus not due to infiltrating cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the CD45/CD31 double staining data

claim: 94% of CD31+ cells expressed GFP protein before MI in tamoxifen-injected Cdh5:ROSA26 mice

evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C

claim: Almost all CD31+ cells expressed the GFP protein in the ZI+BZ and RZ of BNP-treated and untreated infarcted hearts 10 days after MI
